items.content: The coffee had been brewing since before anyone woke, its dark breath filling the kitchen like a quiet announcement. Steam curled from the pot in slow, unhurried spirals, dissolving into the pale light that crept beneath the curtains. There was something almost mournful in it — the smell of readiness, of a day insisting on beginning whether you were prepared or not. She stood in the doorway, still half a dream, and let it reach her.

items.content: The train moved through country she had never seen before, past fields that seemed to belong to some older, quieter version of the world. Farmhouses slid by like thoughts she couldn't quite hold onto, and the sky above them was the pale, indifferent grey of early afternoon. She pressed her forehead against the cool glass and felt, strangely, that she was not travelling toward anything but simply passing through the long, unhurried middle of something she couldn't yet name.

items.content: She found it tucked inside a copy of Middlemarch, folded into quarters so many times the creases had gone soft as cloth. The handwriting belonged to her mother — she recognized the particular lean of the letters, the way certain words pressed harder into the page, as though urgency itself had weight. She read it twice before understanding that it had never been meant for her, and a third time before realizing it had always been.
